reading.body:
CyrusOne's Chandler campus publishes 169 MW of IT capacity, a third of Arizona's disclosed 512 MW, while most of the state's 57 mapped data centers publish no power figure at all.

The disclosure gap is the story. Four Arizona facilities publish capacity numbers, and one of them, this eight-building campus, accounts for 33 percent of the disclosed total. The campus covers 2 million square feet of technical space and carries certifications for regulated work, including SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, FISMA, ISO 27001, and TIA-942. Those qualifications say the campus can host financial, healthcare, and government tenants. They do not say which tenants are there.

For AI specifically, the megawatt figure is the useful part and the rack math shows why. At 40 kW per rack, a common training density, 169 MW is roughly 4,200 racks. At 10 kW per rack for inference, the same power supports roughly 16,900 racks. Identical capacity, four times the rack count, and very different amounts of compute. A published megawatt number bounds the electrical load a campus can place on the grid, which is the constraint that matters for siting and power procurement. It does not tell you how much AI hardware is installed or running.

What the data does not cover is large. There are no coordinates, no tenant names, no utilization figures, and no announced expansion, which the suitability score of 83 lists as its missing input. That score rests only on published IT capacity and operator type. The 512 MW state figure is a floor built from four disclosures, not a total, and the 57 mapped facilities without power figures could hold substantially more load than the ones that report it.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
